key: He did not transfer his anger; he did not repeat a fault.
s: Asked by the Duke Ai who loved learning, Confucius names Yen Hui; He Yan, on 6.2, reads him as led by the Way where ordinary men follow feeling, his anger kept to its due and never shifted, and no wrong ever done twice.

evidence.words: 凡人任情，喜怒違理。顔淵任道，怒不過分。遷者，移也。怒當其理，不移易也。不貳過者，有不善，未嘗復行。
evidence.gloss: Ordinary people give rein to feeling, and their joy and anger go against principle. Yan Yuan gave himself to the Way, and his anger did not exceed its due. To transfer is to shift: his anger fitted its reason and did not shift. Not repeating a fault: when he did something not good, he never did it again.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Analects 6.2, at 120). The packet’s He Yan text (revision 2270601) gives one gloss on 6.2 with no author tag, which under the plan’s rule is He Yan’s own, so naming He Yan directly is correct. It contrasts ordinary men who follow feeling with Yan Yuan who follows the Way, says his anger did not exceed its due and did not shift, and glosses not repeating a fault as never doing a wrong twice; the reading paraphrases this without addition. Plain sense is faithful: the Duke Ai asks which disciple loved to learn and Confucius names Yen Hui. Source line matches the packet edition and revision. entry-check ok.
